title: At the Pharmacy
objectives: Ask about medications and side effects
target_phrases: I need to fill this prescription

dialogue.title: Filling a Prescription
dialogue.context: Ahmed goes to the pharmacy to fill his prescription for antibiotics. He asks the pharmacist questions about the medication.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Hello, I need to fill this prescription from Dr. Chen.

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.text: Sure, let me take a look. Okay, this is for amoxicillin, an antibiotic. Do you have insurance?

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.text: Great. With insurance, your copay is $10. It'll be ready in about 15 minutes. Is this your first time taking this medication?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Yes, it is. How do I take it?

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.text: Take one capsule twice a day - once in the morning and once in the evening. Take it with food to avoid stomach upset. Make sure you finish all 20 capsules even if you feel better.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Okay. Are there any side effects I should know about?

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.text: Common side effects include mild stomach upset or diarrhea. If you develop a rash, severe stomach pain, or trouble breathing, stop taking it and call your doctor immediately.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I understand. Also, do you have something for my cough? Dr. Chen said I could take cough syrup.

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.text: Yes, cough medicine is over-the-counter - you don't need a prescription. This brand works well. Take one tablespoon every 4-6 hours as needed.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Thank you. When can I come back to pick up the antibiotic?

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.text: Give us 15 minutes. I'll text you when it's ready. You can browse the store or wait here.

listening_exercises.transcript: Understanding medication labels is important. The label shows: drug name, dosage (amount to take), frequency (how often), and special instructions (with food, before bed, etc.). Always read the label carefully. If instructions say 'Take 2 tablets 3 times daily,' that means 2 tablets in the morning, 2 at midday, and 2 in the evening - total of 6 tablets per day.
listening_exercises.question: If medicine says 'Take 2 tablets 3 times daily,' how many tablets do you take per day?

listening_exercises.transcript: Generic vs. brand name medications: Generic medicines have the same active ingredient as brand names but cost less. For example, ibuprofen is the generic name, while Advil and Motrin are brand names. Generics are FDA-approved and just as effective. Ask your pharmacist if a generic version is available to save money.
listening_exercises.question: What's the difference between generic and brand name medicine?
options: Generic is the same but costs less

listening_exercises.transcript: Over-the-counter (OTC) medicines don't require a prescription. Common OTC medicines include pain relievers (acetaminophen, ibuprofen), cold and allergy medicine, antacids for stomach upset, and cough syrup. Even though they're OTC, follow dosage instructions carefully. Some OTC medicines shouldn't be mixed with prescription drugs - always ask your pharmacist.
listening_exercises.question: What does OTC mean?

speaking_tasks.prompt: You're at the pharmacy. Say: 'I need to fill this prescription. How much will it cost with insurance? When will it be ready?' Record yourself.
speaking_tasks.example: Hello, I need to fill this prescription that my doctor gave me. It's for an antibiotic. I have insurance - here's my card. Can you tell me how much my copay will be? Also, how long will it take to get the medication ready? I can wait if it's not too long. Thank you.

speaking_tasks.prompt: Ask the pharmacist 3 questions about a new medication you're taking. Record for 20 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: I have a few questions about this medication. First, should I take it with food or on an empty stomach? Second, are there any side effects I should watch out for? And third, can I drink alcohol while taking this medicine? I want to make sure I take it correctly.

writing_tasks.prompt: Write instructions for taking medicine: 2 capsules, twice a day, with food, for 10 days. (30-40 words)
writing_tasks.example: Take two capsules twice daily - once in the morning and once in the evening. Always take with food to prevent stomach upset. Continue for the full 10 days even if you start feeling better. Don't skip doses. Store at room temperature.

writing_tasks.prompt: You're traveling and need a refill of your medication early. Write what you'd say to the pharmacist. (40-50 words)
writing_tasks.example: Hello, I have a prescription for blood pressure medication that I refill here monthly. I'm going out of town for three weeks and I'll run out while I'm gone. Is it possible to get an early refill so I have enough medication for my trip? I can show you my travel tickets if needed.

grammar_focus.title: 'How often' and 'How much' for Dosage
grammar_focus.explanation: Use 'How often' for frequency and 'How much' for quantity.
examples: How often do I take this? - Twice a day. (frequency)
How much should I take? - Two tablets. (quantity)
How often should I apply this cream? - Every 4 hours. (frequency)
How much medicine per dose? - 5 milliliters. (quantity)

grammar_focus.title: 'Should/Shouldn't' for Recommendations
grammar_focus.explanation: Use 'should' for recommendations and 'shouldn't' for things to avoid.
examples: You should take this with food. (recommendation)
You shouldn't drive after taking this. (avoid)
Should I avoid alcohol? (asking)
You should finish all the pills. (advice)

grammar_focus.title: 'Before' and 'After' for Timing
grammar_focus.explanation: Use 'before' and 'after' to describe when to take medicine.
examples: Take this before meals. (timing)
Take this after eating. (timing)
Use this cream before bed. (timing)
Take your medicine after breakfast. (timing)

cultural_notes: Chain pharmacies like CVS, Walgreens, and Rite Aid are common in the U.S.
Most pharmacies have a drive-through window where you can pick up prescriptions without going inside.
Many pharmacies are open 24 hours, especially in cities.
You can transfer prescriptions between pharmacies if you move or want to change pharmacies.
Pharmacists can give advice about OTC medicines and minor health issues for free.
Insurance copays for prescriptions vary - some are $5, others can be $50+ depending on your plan.
